label: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems
claim: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.
quote: And the crucial point is that I believe that this universality extends not only across simple programs, but also to systems in nature.
scope: simple programs and natural systems with different underlying components
measurable_quantities: qualitative and statistical similarity of patterns produced by natural systems and by simple programs
candidate_data: Published image collections of natural patterns (e.g. shells, crystals, fluid flows) compared against enumerations of simple programs computed in public software.

label: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness
claim: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.
quote: But from my investigations of simple programs I have come to the conclusion that one can in fact identify just three basic mechanisms for randomness, as illustrated in the pictures below.
scope: all systems, natural or computational, that show apparent randomness
candidate_data: none known

label: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature
claim: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.
quote: I believe that this mechanism is in fact ultimately responsible for a large fraction, if not essentially all, of the randomness that we see in the natural world.
scope: random-looking phenomena in the natural world
measurable_quantities: fraction of observed natural random phenomena attributable to intrinsic generation versus external noise or initial conditions
run-to-run repeatability of random details
candidate_data: Replicate-run data from controlled physics, chemistry and fluid experiments, such as the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database for turbulent flows.

label: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness
claim: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.
quote: But despite such sensitivity to microscopic effects, what has consistently been found in practice is that the output from such devices has significant deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: physical random number generators based on electronic or other environmental noise
measurable_quantities: bias and serial correlation of raw hardware generator output
statistical test failure rates before post-processing
candidate_data: Raw output from hardware random number generators analysed with standard test suites such as NIST SP 800-22, TestU01 or Dieharder.

label: Sensitive dependence alone does not make behavior random
claim: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions, as in chaos theory, does not by itself make a system behave randomly; it only makes ever-less-significant digits of the initial conditions matter, so the behavior is random only if those digit sequences are random, and there is no reason to assume the numbers occurring in nature have random digits.
quote: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions thus does not in and of itself imply that a system will behave in a random way.
scope: chaotic dynamical systems such as the doubling (shift) map
measurable_quantities: randomness of trajectories of the doubling map for initial conditions with random versus regular digit sequences
candidate_data: Direct computation of shift-map trajectories with exact arithmetic in standard mathematical software.

label: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps
claim: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is set by the separation between observed large-scale and uncontrollable small-scale features.
quote: So the idea that randomness comes purely from initial conditions can be realistic only for a fairly small number of steps; randomness which is seen after that must therefore typically be attributed to other mechanisms.
scope: physical systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions
measurable_quantities: number of amplification steps or collisions before trajectories are dominated by environmental perturbations
ratio of observed to microscopic length scales
candidate_data: Experimental trajectory data from Galton-board, billiard or chaotic-pendulum experiments with repeated runs.

label: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years
claim: Although planetary motion looks regular on human timescales, sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur in the solar system, producing significant randomness over a few million years that may explain some present-day features of the solar system.
quote: But calculations imply that sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur even in our solar system.
scope: orbital dynamics of planets and other bodies in the solar system
measurable_quantities: Lyapunov time of planetary orbits
divergence of numerical orbit integrations from nearby initial conditions
candidate_data: JPL planetary ephemerides and published long-term numerical integrations of solar system orbits.

label: Rule 30 center column passes all practical tests of randomness
claim: The sequence of center-cell colors produced by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell shows no regularities under any standard statistical, mathematical or perceptual method of analysis, making it at least as random as any phenomenon in nature that is considered random.
quote: But the remarkable fact is that none of these methods seem to reveal any real regularities whatsoever in the rule 30 cellular automaton sequence.
scope: the center column of the rule 30 elementary cellular automaton
measurable_quantities: statistical test results (frequency, runs, spectral, compression) on long stretches of the rule 30 center column
candidate_data: The rule 30 center column tabulated in OEIS or recomputed directly, analysed with test suites such as NIST SP 800-22, TestU01 or Dieharder.

label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
claim: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies regularity.
quote: But in practice over the years, one after another linear congruential generator that has been constructed to have maximal repetition period has turned out to exhibit very substantial deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: linear congruential pseudorandom number generators
measurable_quantities: lattice structure of successive output tuples (spectral test)
statistical test failure rates
candidate_data: Direct computation of generators such as multiplier 65539 (RANDU) and evaluation with the spectral test or TestU01.

label: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness
claim: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.
quote: the very possibility of any detailed mathematical analysis tends to imply the presence of at least some deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: deterministic systems used to generate randomness, including pseudorandom generators
measurable_quantities: statistical quality of output from analytically tractable versus intractable generators
candidate_data: Published comparisons of pseudorandom generators under TestU01 batteries.

label: Rapid production of much randomness indicates intrinsic generation
claim: Whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be responsible, because it uses every component of a system to produce new randomness and has no length limit, whereas environmental amplification is slow and initial-condition randomness is short-lived.
quote: The basic answer, I believe, is that whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be the mechanism responsible.
scope: natural and engineered systems that produce randomness
measurable_quantities: rate of randomness (entropy) production per unit time
dependence of output on environmental isolation
candidate_data: none known

label: Intrinsically generated randomness is repeatable across experimental runs
claim: If randomness in an experiment comes from intrinsic generation, then even the precise details of the random-looking behavior should be repeatable from one run to the next, because such behavior is robust to perturbations below a critical size, whereas randomness from the environment or from initial conditions should show little or no repeatability.
quote: But what is remarkable is that if intrinsic randomness generation is the mechanism at work, then the precise details of the behavior can also be repeatable.
scope: carefully controlled experiments showing random-looking behavior
measurable_quantities: correlation of detailed random features between repeated runs of the same experiment
critical perturbation size below which behavior is unchanged
candidate_data: Replicate-run datasets from controlled fluid, chemical or pattern-formation experiments, where published.

label: Detailed visual similarities in organisms imply intrinsic randomness
claim: Detailed visual similarities between members of the same species, and between the two symmetric sides of a system, in features that look complex and random cannot be attributed to environmental or initial-condition randomness and must come from intrinsic randomness generation.
quote: And instead, there is no choice but to conclude that the randomness must in fact come from the mechanism of intrinsic randomness generation that I have discovered in simple programs, and discussed in this section.
scope: complex-looking patterns in physical, biological and other systems, especially bilaterally symmetric ones
measurable_quantities: similarity of complex pattern details between left and right sides or between conspecific individuals
candidate_data: Published image collections of animal pigmentation and shell patterns allowing left-right and between-individual comparisons.

label: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior
claim: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular automata that grow circular shapes.
quote: But it turns out that all that really seems to matter is that randomness is present: the mechanism through which it arises appears to be largely irrelevant.
scope: discrete systems such as random walks, aggregation models and cellular automata, and fluids made of molecules
measurable_quantities: isotropy and smoothness of large-scale shapes or distributions generated from discrete rules with external versus intrinsic randomness
candidate_data: Direct simulation of random walks, Eden-type models and two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata in public software.

label: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes
claim: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.
quote: In general the point is that continuous behavior can arise in systems with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes.
scope: discrete systems with randomness, including growth processes and domain coarsening
measurable_quantities: ratio of small-scale update rate to large-scale growth or boundary-motion rate
smoothness of resulting large-scale forms
candidate_data: Direct simulation of cellular automata and growth models in public software.

label: Density-driven discrete transitions are rare in 1D CAs, common in higher dimensions
claim: Cellular automata in which a continuous change in initial density of black cells produces a discrete switch in long-time behavior, with whichever color was initially more common taking over the whole system, are fairly rare in one dimension, where domain boundaries often get stuck, but become increasingly common in two and more dimensions.
quote: And so long as the boundaries of the regions do not get stuck—as happens in many one-dimensional cellular automata—the result is that whichever color was initially more common eventually takes over the whole system.
scope: cellular automata in one, two and more dimensions started from random initial conditions of varying density
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules showing a discontinuous dependence of final density on initial density, by dimension
candidate_data: Systematic enumeration and simulation of cellular automaton rule spaces in public software.

label: Continuous rules can yield discrete behavior, so discrete models often fit
claim: Even systems governed by continuous equations, such as certain chemical reaction kinetics, commonly have a limited number of stable states with discrete transitions between them, and because discrete overall behavior is often a system's most obvious feature, discrete models like cellular automata are often the most appropriate.
quote: And in fact it is quite common for such behavior to be one of the most obvious features of a system—which is why discrete systems like cellular automata end up often being the most appropriate models.
scope: natural systems with continuous underlying dynamics but discrete overall behavior, such as phase transitions and bistable chemical reactions
measurable_quantities: number of stable states and sharpness of transitions as parameters vary
candidate_data: Experimental data on bistable chemical reactions and phase transitions in the published literature.

label: Complex natural behavior is almost never best explained by constraints
claim: Almost none of the complex behavior seen in nature is best explained as the satisfaction of constraints, because finding a pattern that satisfies a constraint is usually far too difficult a computation to happen routinely in nature; explicit processes of evolution are the more plausible explanation.
quote: But despite this, my strong suspicion is that of all the examples of complex behavior that we see in nature almost none can in the end best be explained in terms of constraints.
scope: complex behavior in physical and other natural systems
candidate_data: none known

label: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints
claim: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural systems are unlikely to come close to satisfying such constraints.
quote: So what this suggests is that even if in some idealized sense a system in nature might be expected to satisfy certain constraints, it is likely that in practice the system will actually not have a way to come even close to doing this.
scope: iterative and annealing-like procedures for discrete constraint satisfaction, and natural systems assumed to satisfy constraints
measurable_quantities: fraction of constraint violations remaining after a given number of local-update steps
time to reach exact solutions
candidate_data: Direct simulation of local-search procedures on tiling and constraint problems, and published benchmarks for constraint-satisfaction and SAT solvers.

label: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing
claim: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.
quote: But if one just tries pushing balls together they almost always get stuck, and never take on anything like the arrangement shown.
scope: packing of identical spheres and circles under physical compression or agitation
measurable_quantities: packing fraction achieved by compressed or vibrated sphere assemblies versus the face-centered cubic value
degree of crystalline order
candidate_data: Published granular-packing experiments and simulations on random close packing of spheres.

label: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints
claim: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
quote: when more complex forms are seen they once again tend to be associated not with constraints but rather with the effects of explicit evolution rules—mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
scope: biological forms shaped by natural selection and development
measurable_quantities: whether complex biological forms are reproduced by growth-rule models versus optimization/constraint models
candidate_data: Published developmental-biology and morphogenesis datasets such as shell and leaf shape collections.

label: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity
claim: There is no direct correspondence between the complexity of a system's underlying rules and the complexity of its behavior: some of the simplest rules yield highly complex behavior, fairly complicated rules often yield simple behavior, and rules differing at a single position can behave very differently.
quote: Traditional intuition might have made one assume that there must be a direct correspondence between the complexity of observed behavior and the complexity of underlying rules. But one of the central discoveries of this book is that in fact there is not.
scope: simple programs such as cellular automata, and by extension natural systems
measurable_quantities: correlation between rule description length and behavioral complexity measures across enumerated rules
candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration of elementary and other cellular automata computed in public software.

label: Nesting in nature mostly arises from building up, not splitting down
claim: Nested patterns can arise either from elements splitting or branching into smaller ones or from larger elements being built up from smaller ones (as in additive cellular automata), and the building-up route is probably the more common origin of nesting in nature.
quote: it can also arise when larger elements are built up from smaller ones—and indeed I suspect that this is its more common origin in nature.
scope: nested (self-similar) patterns in natural systems
measurable_quantities: developmental or formation history of natural nested structures (splitting versus aggregation)
candidate_data: none known

label: Merging of independently growing domains generically produces nesting
claim: Nesting can arise from random initial conditions through progressive annihilation of randomly placed elements: in essentially any system where domains grow fairly independently and then progressively merge, an overall nested pattern resembling a river-tributary tree forms, even when domain boundaries move as random walks.
quote: And indeed in essentially any system where there are domains that grow fairly independently and then progressively merge the same basic overall nesting will be seen.
scope: cellular automata such as rules 184 and 110 and other domain-coarsening systems from random initial conditions
measurable_quantities: scaling of domain sizes and branching statistics of annihilation trees over time
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 184, rule 110 and annihilating random walks in public software, plus river-network data such as HydroSHEDS for comparison.
